questions.stem: About the faraday and the equivalent, the correct propositions are:
options: The faraday is the electric charge carried by one electron
1 mole of Na⁺ corresponds to 2 Eq
1 mole of Ca²⁺ corresponds to 2 Eq
The equivalent is the amount of a substance that carries one faraday of electric charge
questions.explanation: The faraday is the charge of one MOLE of electrons: 1 F = N_A × e = 96 500 C. One equivalent carries 1 F, so 1 mol of a monovalent ion (Na⁺) is 1 Eq and 1 mol of Ca²⁺ is 2 Eq.

questions.stem: About the equivalent concentration Ce of an ion i of valence zᵢ and molar concentration Cᵢ, the correct propositions are:
options: For an ion of valence −2, Ce = −2Cᵢ
In a solution where [Al³⁺] = 1 mol/l, Ce(Al³⁺) = 3 Eq/l
The equivalent concentration of an ion always equals its molar concentration
questions.explanation: Ce = |zᵢ|Cᵢ, in Eq/l; the absolute value makes it positive for anions (a divalent anion gives Ce = 2Cᵢ). It equals the molar concentration only for monovalent ions, e.g. Al³⁺ at 1 mol/l gives 3 Eq/l.

questions.stem: About the total equivalent concentration of a solution and the electroneutrality condition, the correct propositions are:
options: Ce⁻ = Σ|zᵢ⁻|Cᵢ⁻ is the total equivalent concentration of anions
Electroneutrality requires equal molar concentrations of cations and anions
questions.explanation: Ce = Ce⁺ + Ce⁻ with Ce± = Σ|zᵢ±|Cᵢ±; electroneutrality is Ce⁺ = Ce⁻, hence Ce = 2Ce⁺ = 2Ce⁻. It is the equivalents that balance, not the moles: in 2 mol/l CaCl₂, [Ca²⁺] = 2 mol/l but [Cl⁻] = 4 mol/l.

questions.stem: 1 l of a solution contains 1 mole of Na₂SO₄ and 2 moles of KCl (totally dissociated). The equivalent concentration Ce of this solution is:
questions.explanation: Ce⁺ = 1×[Na⁺] + 1×[K⁺] = 2 + 2 = 4 Eq/l; Ce⁻ = 2×[SO₄²⁻] + 1×[Cl⁻] = 2 + 2 = 4 Eq/l; Ce = 2Ce⁺ = 8 Eq/l. 4 Eq/l is only Ce⁺, and 7 is the total ionic molar concentration (ignores |z|).

questions.stem: 0.5 l of a solution contains 0.1 mole of AlCl₃ (totally dissociated). The correct propositions are:
options: The total ionic molar concentration equals Ce
questions.explanation: [AlCl₃] = 0.1/0.5 = 0.2 mol/l → [Al³⁺] = 0.2 mol/l, [Cl⁻] = 0.6 mol/l. Ce⁺ = 3 × 0.2 = 0.6 Eq/l (not 0.2, which forgets z), Ce⁻ = 0.6 Eq/l, Ce = 1.2 Eq/l, while the ionic molar concentration is only 0.8 mol/l.

questions.stem: Two compartments (1) and (2) of equal volume are separated by a dialysis membrane. (1) contains salt AB at C; (2) contains AB at C and a protein PrBz (Pr^z⁻ + zB⁺) at C′. Initially:
options: A⁻ has a concentration gradient across the membrane
questions.explanation: In (2), B⁺ comes from both AB and PrBz, so [B⁺]₂ = C + zC′ > [B⁺]₁ = C, and B⁺ diffuses from (2) to (1). A⁻ starts at C on both sides (no gradient) yet still moves, dragged by B⁺ for electroneutrality. Pr^z⁻ is non-diffusible.

questions.stem: In the same Donnan experiment (protein Pr^z⁻ in compartment (2)), n moles of B⁺ (x = n/V) have crossed the membrane at equilibrium. The correct propositions are:
questions.explanation: x moles of B⁺ and of A⁻ go from (2) to (1), so [A⁻]₁ = [B⁺]₁ = C + x, [A⁻]₂ = C − x, [B⁺]₂ = C + zC′ − x. Hence [A⁻]₁ > [A⁻]₂ and [B⁺]₂ > [B⁺]₁: same-sign ions end up unequally distributed, with the inverse ratio [A⁻]₂/[A⁻]₁ = [B⁺]₁/[B⁺]₂.

questions.stem: In a Donnan experiment, (1) contains NaCl at C = 0.1 mol/l; (2) contains NaCl at 0.1 mol/l and a protein PrNa₂₀ (z = 20) at C′ = 2 mmol/l. Using x = zCC′/(4C + zC′), the Cl⁻ concentration in (2) at equilibrium is approximately:
In a Donnan experiment (protein anion in compartment (2)), at equilibrium [Na⁺]₁ = [Cl⁻]₁ = 0.15 mol/l and [Na⁺]₂ = 0.18 mol/l. The correct propositions are:
options: The equivalent concentration of the protein ion in (2) is 55 mEq/l
questions.explanation: [Cl⁻]₂/[Cl⁻]₁ = [Na⁺]₁/[Na⁺]₂ gives the equal products, so [Cl⁻]₂ = 0.15²/0.18 = 0.125 mol/l, lower than in (1). Electroneutrality in (2): [Na⁺]₂ = [Cl⁻]₂ + z[Pr] → z[Pr] = 0.18 − 0.125 = 0.055 Eq/l = 55 mEq/l.

questions.stem: The figure shows a Donnan set-up: the macro-ion Pr^z⁻ is retained in compartment (2) and E is the transmembrane electric field. The correct propositions are:
options: The side of the membrane in contact with (2) is negatively charged
The membrane potential V₂ − V₁ is positive
The electric field always points from (+) to (−)
questions.explanation: Pr^z⁻ attracts B⁺ and repels A⁻, so the side in contact with (2) is negative and the side facing (1) positive. E points from (+) to (−), i.e. from (1) to (2), so V₁ > V₂ and V₂ − V₁ < 0.

questions.stem: About the Nernst equation, the correct propositions are:
options: It applies to the non-diffusible ions
kT/ze = RT/zF because F = N_A·e and R = N_A·k
In E = −(V₂ − V₁)/l, l is the membrane thickness
questions.explanation: The lesson writes the Nernst equation for diffusible ions as V₂ − V₁ = −(RT/zF)ln(C₂/C₁), equivalently −(kT/ze)ln(C₂/C₁), since F = N_A·e and R = N_A·k. E = −(V₂ − V₁)/l with l the membrane thickness. It does not apply to the retained Pr^z⁻.

questions.stem: At 37°C, the Cl⁻ concentration is 100 mmol/l in compartment (1) and 10 mmol/l in compartment (2). Using the Nernst equation (R = 8.31 SI, F = 96 500 C/mol), the potential V₂ − V₁ for Cl⁻ is approximately:
questions.explanation: V₂ − V₁ = −(RT/zF)ln(C₂/C₁) with z = −1: = +(8.31 × 310/96 500) × ln(0.1) = 0.0267 × (−2.303) ≈ −61.5 mV. +61.5 mV forgets that z = −1 for Cl⁻, ±26.7 mV uses log₁₀ instead of ln, and −59.5 mV uses 300 K instead of 310 K.

questions.stem: About the Donnan (Gibbs–Donnan) equilibrium equation, the correct propositions are:
options: It is obtained by writing that two diffusible ions see the same potential V₂ − V₁
Applied to A⁻ and B⁺, it gives [A⁻]₂/[A⁻]₁ = [B⁺]₂/[B⁺]₁
(1/z)·ln([I]₂/[I]₁) = (1/z′)·ln([I′]₂/[I′]₁) for two diffusible ions I and I′
It can be written with equivalent concentrations: (1/z)·ln(Ce₂(I)/Ce₁(I)) = (1/z′)·ln(Ce₂(I′)/Ce₁(I′))
It is applied to the non-diffusible macro-ion Pr^z⁻
questions.explanation: Equating the Nernst expressions of V₂ − V₁ for two diffusible ions gives (1/z)ln([I]₂/[I]₁) = (1/z′)ln([I′]₂/[I′]₁); since Ce = |z|[I], the same ratio holds with Ce. With z = −1 and +1 it gives the INVERSE ratio [A⁻]₂/[A⁻]₁ = [B⁺]₁/[B⁺]₂.

questions.stem: Which of the following solutions (totally dissociated) have a total equivalent concentration Ce = 2 Eq/l?
questions.explanation: Ce = 2Ce⁺. NaCl 1 mol/l: Ce⁺ = 1 → 2 Eq/l. CaCl₂ 0.5 mol/l: Ce⁺ = 2 × 0.5 = 1 → 2 Eq/l. AlCl₃ 1/3 mol/l: Ce⁺ = 3 × 1/3 = 1 → 2 Eq/l. CaCl₂ 1 mol/l gives 4 Eq/l and NaCl 0.5 mol/l gives 1 Eq/l.
